text:
Most people think building an AI agent requires a team of developers.

It doesn’t always.

You can start with a simple structure and let Claude handle more of the repetitive work.

This 6-step workflow shows how:

1. Install Claude Code
Choose the interface that fits your workflow — terminal, desktop or VS Code.

2. Build context
Create a "CLAUDE.md" file with your role, voice, rules, preferences and project context.

3. Build memory
Turn corrections into reusable memory so Claude doesn’t keep making the same mistakes.

4. Build skills
Package repetitive workflows into reusable commands that can connect with tools like Notion, Gmail and Drive.

5. Build agents
Give different agents specific jobs — strategist, builder, analyst, reviewer — instead of making one agent do everything.

6. Run on autopilot
Use scheduled routines to let your workflows run automatically and deliver the output where you need it.

The bigger idea isn’t:

“How do I make Claude write code?”

It’s:

“How do I build a system where Claude can understand, remember, execute and improve?”

That’s the difference between using AI as a chatbot…

…and building an AI-powered workflow around your business.

You don’t need to automate everything on day one.

Start with one repetitive task.

Turn it into a skill.

Then connect the next one.

Save this framework if you want to start building AI agents.

Follow @AamirAnsar94694 for more practical AI, tech & automation insights.

#AI #Claude #AIAgents #ClaudeCode #Automation #AITools #ArtificialIntelligence #FutureOfWork

text:
Six weeks is enough to get certified as a Claude Architect if you follow the order and do not skip ahead.

Week 1 is coursework only: Building with the Claude API, Introduction to Model Context Protocol, Claude Code in Action, Claude 101. Skipping this step is how people show up to the exam knowing prompts but not the system underneath them.

Week 2 turns that coursework into real projects using Claude Code, the Agent SDK, the Anthropic API, and MCP. Reading about a tool and building with it are not the same skill, and the exam tests the second one.

Week 3 shifts from building to the exam itself: go through all six exam scenarios, get familiar with the five domains, and learn exactly which skills each task assessment is checking for.

Week 4 is where the real preparation happens. Build a multi-tool agent with escalation logic, configure Claude Code for a team development workflow, build a structured data extraction pipeline, and design and debug a multi-agent research pipeline. These four exercises mirror what the actual exam asks for.

Week 5 is a practice exam. Aim for a score above 850 out of 1000 before moving on.

Week 6 is the real exam, and you only get one attempt.

Bookmark this roadmap if certification is on your list this year.

text:
I hate building frontends with AI.

Claude, Codex, and Kimi can generate a dashboard in 30 seconds. Then I spend the next six hours explaining that the main button is invisible, the table breaks on mobile, and every screen looks like the same pile of rounded cards.

I've installed the design skills. I've fed it screenshots from Linear and Stripe. I've used the “premium, minimal, Apple-level” prompts.

It helps. It never removes the babysitting.

AI is incredible at writing frontend code. It is still terrible at knowing when a product feels cheap, confusing, or annoying to use.

One-shot AI frontend design is a lie.

The first 70% takes 30 seconds.

The last 30% ruins your Saturday.

The enterprise AI stack is being rebuilt.

Models are becoming more capable, and increasingly interchangeable. As AI moves from answering questions to doing mission-critical work, the constraint is no longer raw intelligence. It is organizational context: understanding how a company operates, what information matters, and what should happen next.

Without that context, enterprises get shallow answers, rising token costs from sending irrelevant information to expensive models, and AI sprawl as teams adopt disconnected tools. The answer is not simply more models. It is an intelligence layer that understands the organization and routes each task to the right model, agent, and workflow.

That is the thesis behind the 50+ new features we’re announcing today at @Glean:GO, including:
𝗚𝗹𝗲𝗮𝗻 𝗧𝗮𝘂: A new governed desktop AI workspace that combines an open agent harness with your enterprise context, unifying local files, applications, browser workflows, and code repositories in one workspace. That context is what lets agents delegate complex, multi-step work and deliver better performance, while respecting permissions.

𝗚𝗹𝗲𝗮𝗻 𝗜𝗻𝘁𝗲𝗹𝗹𝗶𝗴𝗲𝗻𝗰𝗲: Uses organizational context to route each task to the right model, while giving enterprises control over quality, usage, and cost. Our benchmark found that Glean reduced token costs by 81% as compared to Claude Cowork, and was preferred 78% of the time.

𝗚𝗹𝗲𝗮𝗻 𝗧𝗿𝗮𝗻𝘀𝗳𝗼𝗿𝗺: Built on your Enterprise Graph, it understands how work happens across your organization, identifies the best opportunities for AI, recommends the right agents and skills, and measures the impact on your business. 

To help us announce these new capabilities, I’m looking forward to being joined by leaders from some of the world’s most innovative organizations, including @GM, @nvidia, @Snowflake, and @OpenAI, who will share how they are using Glean in mission-critical workflows.

See you today at Glean:GO in San Francisco and online.

The photo above is a coding harness tier list... and I somewhat agree with it.

However, Hermes Agent @NousResearch  in particular is sits a tier above even the top tier.

While I respect tools like omp and Claude Code, I feel like you only need this one. So I wrapped it into oh-my-hermes and optimized it with engineering coding tools and a memory system.

Maintaining codebase quality is crucial, and so is sharing context with the user. If the harness and model output bad code, they will generate even worse code on top of it, causing the system to collapse over time. I let it run with clearly defined quality Evals and goal baselines, and I have also embedded reinforced software architecture thinking—like OCP, coupling, and modular interface design.

Code search efficiency is boosted by ast-grep, sub-agent routing directs tasks to the right models, and specialized prompting skills leverage the unique strengths of each model (Opus, GPT, Kimi, Fable, GLM, DeepSeek, Qwen, Grok, Gemini...). It also features parallel tool calling & Eval execution, long-term memory labeling (Fact, decision, episode, representation, TTL), and built-in interview skills for memory consolidation—all packed into a Power Intelligence Plugin for hermes-agent.

I'm maxing out tens of billions of tokens using strictly this. Still have a Claude subscription instead of Nous Portal? Don't worry—just have Hermes trigger Claude and aggregate the results; I've baked in all those rules. Design skills, Ops skills—there are just tons of them.

So now I work exclusively with Hermes Agent. I highly recommend subscribing to Nous Portal because I've fine-tuned task routing based on what each model does best. Since it supports multiple models, you can cancel your Claude or Codex subscriptions and just use this.
